name: energy
title: Track your electricity or your fuel
pitch: How much do you really use each month, and what does it cost? You enter your meter readings or your fill-ups; the program keeps them in a file and shows you the months, the averages and the trend.

steps.do: Choose what you track: electricity meter readings, or fill-ups (date, liters, price, kilometers). Write 3 readings in your code and print them.
steps.hint: Plain variables and `printf` are enough for now. `%.2f` prints two decimals.
steps.why: Real numbers from your own life make it easy to see if a result is wrong.

steps.do: Put one reading in a struct, and keep them in an array.
steps.hint: `struct reading { char date[11]; double value; };` and an array of them.
steps.why: A struct groups the fields that belong together, so one reading travels as one thing. It's C's way to describe your data.

steps.do: Compute what you used between two readings (kWh, or liters per 100 km).
steps.done: the result matches your own calculation on paper.
steps.hint: Subtract the previous reading from the current one. For fuel: liters × 100 / kilometers driven.
steps.why: Checking a program against a calculation made by hand is the simplest test there is, and it catches real bugs.

steps.do: Read a new reading typed by the user, and check it: a date, positive numbers, a meter that doesn't go backwards.
steps.done: a wrong value is refused with a clear message.
steps.hint: `fgets` reads a whole line safely, then `sscanf` takes the values out of it and returns how many it found.
steps.why: `scanf` alone leaves junk in the input when it fails. Reading a line, then parsing it, keeps the input under control.

steps.do: Save the readings to a CSV file, and load them at start.
steps.done: your readings are still there after restarting.
steps.hint: `fprintf(f, "%s,%.2f\n", …)` to write; `fgets` + `sscanf` with a comma in the format to read.
steps.why: CSV is plain text: you can open it in a spreadsheet, check it by eye, or fix it in an editor.

steps.do: Print the use and the cost for each month.
steps.done: one line per month, and the total of the year.
steps.hint: The month is the first 7 characters of an ISO date (2026-10). `strncmp` compares the start of two strings.
steps.why: Grouping by month is the same idea as grouping by theme in any language: a key, and a running total.

steps.do: Print the average, the best and the worst month.
steps.done: they match what you see in the monthly list.
steps.hint: One loop: keep the smallest and largest seen so far, and the sum.
steps.why: One pass over the data, a few variables that remember: an algorithm you'll write many times.

steps.do: Let the list grow without a fixed size, with malloc and realloc.
steps.done: 1000 readings load without a crash, and valgrind reports no leaks.
steps.hint: Start with room for 16, double it with `realloc` when it's full, `free` at the end. Run `valgrind ./energy`.
steps.why: Fixed arrays break the day your data grows. Doubling the size when it's full is the trick behind most growable lists, in every language.

steps.do: Handle a broken line in the file (a missing field, a letter instead of a number).
steps.done: the program says which line is wrong and keeps the others.
steps.hint: Count lines as you read, and check what `sscanf` returns.
steps.why: Files get edited by hand and get damaged. Telling the user the line number makes the problem easy to fix.

steps.do: Optional: a bar chart of the months made of # characters.
steps.done: the chart shows your winter months taller (or your holiday trips).
steps.hint: Scale each month to the biggest one: `width = value * 40 / max`.
steps.why: A picture shows a trend faster than a column of numbers, even one made of # characters.
